label: Dynamical Systems
notes: Open by framing the appendix: a dynamical system is just a vector field on a manifold together with the flow it generates. Stress that classical mechanics is one privileged corner of this larger qualitative theory, and that today we trade explicit solutions for geometric pictures of long-term behaviour.

label: Vector Fields and Phase Flow
notes: Define the phase flow as the one-parameter group obtained by integrating the field. Emphasize the group laws and existence-uniqueness as the reason orbits never cross. Point at the streamlines: each curve is one solution, and the field is tangent to it everywhere along the motion.

label: Fixed Points and Linearization
notes: Explain that equilibria are zeros of the field and that the Jacobian governs nearby motion. Introduce the Hartman-Grobman idea informally: away from eigenvalues on the imaginary axis, the nonlinear flow looks like its linear part. This justifies reading eigenvalues to classify behaviour.

label: Eigenvalue Classification
notes: Walk the eigenvalue plane: real same-sign gives nodes, real opposite-sign gives saddles, complex with nonzero real part gives foci, pure imaginary gives centers. Connect each case to a sketch and stress that sign of the real part decides attraction versus repulsion, the master stability question.

label: The Saddle Portrait
notes: This is the visual centerpiece. Trace the stable manifold as the set flowing into the saddle, the unstable manifold as the set flowing out, and the hyperbolic curves squeezing between them. Contrast with the spiralling focus inset so students feel the difference between saddle and focus geometry.

label: Stable and Unstable Manifolds
notes: Promote the eigendirections to invariant manifolds tangent to the linear eigenspaces. Note that they are global objects, often curved, and that their intersections create the homoclinic tangles behind chaos. Mention the stable manifold theorem as the rigorous backbone of the picture just drawn.

label: Periodic Orbits and Limit Cycles
notes: Distinguish a closed orbit from a limit cycle, which is an isolated closed orbit attracting or repelling its neighbours. Give the van der Pol oscillator as the canonical example and emphasize that limit cycles are a genuinely nonlinear phenomenon absent from linear systems.

label: The Poincare Return Map
notes: This is the second key visual. Introduce a transverse section and the first-return map sending a point to where its orbit next pierces the section. Explain that a periodic orbit becomes a fixed point of this map, reducing flow analysis by one dimension and converting stability into a derivative.

label: Structural Stability and Bifurcations
notes: Define structural stability as robustness of the phase portrait under small perturbations of the field. Then bifurcations are the breakdown points where portraits change qualitatively. Sketch the saddle-node and Hopf as the prototypes, and connect Hopf to the birth of a limit cycle from a focus.

label: Invariant Sets and Attractors
notes: Build the hierarchy of long-term objects: invariant sets, then attractors as the sets that capture open neighbourhoods of initial data. Mention fixed points, limit cycles, tori, and strange attractors as members. Stress that attractors organize the asymptotic fate of almost every trajectory.

label: Integrable versus Chaotic
notes: Contrast regular motion on invariant tori, where action-angle variables linearize the flow, with chaotic motion showing sensitive dependence and positive Lyapunov exponents. Frame this as the central tension of the theory and the reason mechanics needs both integrable models and chaos.

label: Mechanics as a Special Case
notes: Close by placing Hamiltonian flows inside the general theory. Highlight the symplectic constraints: volume preservation forbids attractors, centers replace foci, and energy levels foliate phase space. Recap the toolkit, linearization, sections, manifolds, and bifurcations, as the lens for the rest of the book.
